hint.text: MPs (Members of Parliament) are members of the House of Commons, and peers are members of the House of Lords.
hint.label: MPs and peers

atoms.text: The government consists of ministers of the leading party. The prime minister is the head of government and appoints MPs and peers to become ministers. Every minister is responsible for a certain department.

The most high-ranking ministers in charge of the most important departments, such as national defence, education or finance, are part of the cabinet together with the prime minister. The cabinet meets once a week and regularly discusses their actions with Parliament. Outer ministers are not part of the cabinet and do not attend cabinet meetings.

The parties that did not get into government form the opposition. The largest opposition party is known as the “official opposition”. Just as the government has a cabinet, the “official opposition” has a shadow cabinet consisting of the leader of the opposition and shadow ministers. The opposition has no executive power. Its job is to question the government's decisions and to hold them accountable.

atoms.a: Who is the leader of the government?

b: ++To observe the government's decisions and criticise them if necessary.
To appoint ministers of the cabinet.
To carry out laws just like the government does.

atoms.a: Whom does the prime minister appoint as ministers?
Which party/parties is/are represented in the government?
What differences are there between senior and outer ministers?
b: ++Only senior ministers may attend cabinet meetings.
++The departments of senior ministers are regarded as more important.
Outer ministers are appointed by the leader of the opposition.
Members of any party can become outer ministers.

hint.label: Vocabulary

atoms.b: The government decides how to manage the country. This includes setting ((++taxes laws ballots)) and choosing what the money is spent on, creating a foreign policy for international relations and running important ((++public_services news_channels courts)). Government ministers must regularly present their decisions to Parliament, where they are asked questions and ((++criticised applauded supported)) if necessary.

The government needs the ((++Parliament courts cabinet))'s trust. If the majority vote they have no confidence in the government, the ((++ministers MPs Lords)), including the prime minister, must resign. Similarly, the prime minister may dissolve Parliament at any time. In both cases, new general elections must be held. If that happens, everyone will lose their office except for the ((++peers MPs senior_ministers)) that have been appointed for life.

Bills can be introduced by the government or any of the chambers in ((++Parliament cabinet church)). However, in order to become a law, a bill has to be approved by both the ((++House_of_Commons prime_minister government)) and the ((++House_of_Lords cabinet monarch)), as they represent the legislative branch. They also have the power to ((++amend propose deny)) existing laws.

instruction.text: Answer the questions. Only one answer is correct.

atoms.text: While Parliament and government are closely intertwined, the courts have a more independent role. The system of courts consists of a hierarchy with the Supreme Court at the top. The judges take care of all sorts of civil and criminal cases. Highly serious or significant cases are handled by higher courts. Judges in high courts are called justices. The courts are also responsible for ensuring that the actions of government and Parliament are constitutional.

b: The only court in the UK.
An institution closely intertwined with government and Parliament.
++The highest court in the UK court system.

atoms.a: What are members of courts called?
How do the courts influence the government and Parliament?
b: ++By making sure their actions do not go against the constitution.
